The great migration

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why are South Africans emigrating in their droves and where are they going?

Unique Selling Point:
For the first time ever more Black professionals are leaving the country than their White compatriots. We find out why?

Summary:
According to FNB's Home Sales survey the number of South Africans selling their homes because they are emigrating has doubled in the last two years. What effect does this have on the housing market?
ADVTech is the coding company for private school groups Crawford College and Abbotts College. Their earnings are down 30% due to families emigrating.

Press Release:


The Great Migration
From medical doctors, engineers to finance specialists – skilled and educated South Africans are packing it all up and heading abroad. With the high crime rate, loss of job security and economic uncertainty thousands are looking for greener pastures and the United Kingdom and Australia seem to be the destinations of choice. But what impact will the loss of these critical skills have on South Africa? And who is coming in from elsewhere to work in SA? Carte Blanche explores the great migration.
Producer: Kate Barry
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


LEAVING SA

V/O: They say living in South Africa is like having a luxury suite - on the Titanic. But many educated passengers seem to be jumping ship.

Vox: The way things are going now, gonna be sooner than later.

Vox: Next plane, I’m gone.

Link: Sunshine, clean air, unmatched natural beauty – you’d think that you’d never want to leave – and yet South Africans are leaving our shores in droves. Exactly why, and where are they going to?

Megan: We always planned to stay in South Africa, but as soon as we had our son, we took a step back and looked at the bigger picture.

V/O: Dr Megan Laird is a marine biologist from Cape Town. She and her family will be emigrating in a few weeks’ time.

Megan: We’re concerned about education in this country, we’re concerned about crime, and we just want to give him all the opportunities that we can and we are able to. So basically, we decided to go to New Zealand.

Derek: Was it difficult to get work overseas, especially in New Zealand?

Megan: It is a challenge, but because my husband is in a trade it was easier for him. So we applied through his plumbing qualifications and he got a job on the first day he was there. So there definitely are a lot of jobs out there, and they’re in need of people. So they’re encouraging people to apply.

Link: According to a recent Estate Agent’s Survey, more than 14% of all house sales are emigration-driven. That might not sound like a lot, but it’s up from 10% at the end of last year, and double what it was 2 years ago.

V/O: Biddulph’s is a privately-owned removals company. According to their records many more people are leaving, says Managing Director Owen Farmerey.

Owen: By about 2013 we'd actually seen a huge increase in terms of people returning to South Africa. And at that point for every 10 people we're shipping out we were bringing 15 back. And from there on out we actually saw a noticeable increase in terms of people emigrating. So at this stage probably about 45 percent more than in 2015.

Derek: Where are your clients moving to?

Owen: We are looking at the key destinations being the United Kingdom, followed by probably Australia, then New Zealand and the United States of America.

V/O: But nobody seems to know exactly how many people are leaving. In 2017 America’s PEW Research Center reported 900 000 South Africans living abroad, but Homecoming Revolution, the global headhunting firm for Africa, claims the true figure is 2.7 million.

Sihle: The truth is there is an increase on South Africans who are emigrating to other countries, mostly developed countries, OECD countries.

V/O: Sihle Mthiyane is the Acting Chief Director of Policy for the Department of Home Affairs.

Derek: Does Home Affairs know how many South Africans have emigrated in the last 5 or 10 years?

Sihle: There is no accurate study which will tell you exact figures of people who have been, who are leaving the country.

V/O: But ask the Australians and they’ll tell you exactly how many of us have moved there. 162 448 South Africans were living Down Under in 2016. 67% of them had tertiary qualifications.

Derek: Are you very concerned about the Brain Drain?

Sihle: Very much so. For us to be able to invest in our economy we need skilled people, we need professionals.

Derek: Is it fair to say that a relatively unskilled person from Zimbabwe can get into this country easier than a highly skilled person from Europe?

Sihle: You have a list of occupations that are in high demand in the country. As long as you are on the list, you are able to come to South Africa.
V/O: In 2017, the Department of Home Affairs published a White Paper on International Migration. It claims that more black professionals are leaving South Africa, than white.
Text: …white emigrants appear to be outnumbered by growing numbers of black professionals who have joined the global skills market.
Derek: I don’t think we should be surprised by those numbers. In South Africa we’ve got more blacks than whites. We are losing black professionals.

V/O: Whether it’s high levels crime, a culture of corruption, dwindling job opportunities or a struggling economy, not all South Africans are leaving for the same reason.

Promise: My husband got shot in 2016 in an attempted hijacking I was pregnant at the time with my second child, and nearly losing him and facing the reality of being a single mother because of crime, it was just crazy. We took him to the clinic after being shot and they did nothing. We were like No we can't live like this. We can we can’t do this.

V/O: Thlologelo Promise Rampa is a social worker with a master’s degree from Wits University. She was unemployed for 3 years before emigrating to Australia with her veterinarian husband and children. The first job she applied for, she got.

Promise: And you find out that they really do value our skills this side, they really do want people who are skilled. So you come from a country, you're a social worker and they don't appreciate you, and have a country that's like Hey I can give you some love.

Derek: You feel wanted?

Promise: I’m so happy. My children are getting the best education for free. I don’t have to sell my kidney! It is much safer, you can leave the car open and no one is going to break in. It’s just so…I’m happy.

Link: It’s skills and money that are leaving the country. For every professional person coming to South Africa, it’s estimated that 8 are leaving. And over a 5-year period we lost a quarter of our super wealthy individuals. Now these are the filthy rich, with a net worth of over $5 million, more than R70 million.

Dawie: A politician will say something populist for example, and the very next day I will start getting emails; very wealthy individuals would ask me to structure certain investments for them abroad. Many of them stay in South Africa to run their businesses, because it can be quite profitable to do business in South Africa. But many of them send their kids or their families out of South Africa.

V/O: Chief economist Dawie Roodt believes the Rand is a hugely undervalued currency.

Dawie: The Rand should in fact be trading at about eight Rand or so to the U.S. dollar. And the fact that the Rand is trading closer to 14 to the U.S. dollar is an indication to the extent of money or capital that has already fled South Africa, pushing the Rand to these very, very weak levels.

Derek: We’re told that more and more black professionals are leaving the country – finding work abroad?

Dawie: I’ve found that many young people of all races are wanting to emigrate from South Africa - not necessarily not ever coming back again. Many of them emigrate, which is a good thing, and come back with experience. But, without a doubt this is not only a white flight thing anymore. All the races today want to see they can get a better future somewhere else.

V/O: Nompakamiso Hude is living the dream in New York City. Originally from Khayalitsha, she’s now a brand manager for global drinks giant Diageo.

Mpaki: I wanted to explore the world. I wanted to see what else is out there beyond South Africa. You know I used to go to the beach and wonder what's happening overseas you know. And when I got that opportunity to be able to move to New York I took it. I grabbed it and I left. I think it is a case of young South Africans wanting bigger and better opportunities and then get those expertise overseas and bring them back.

Derek: So you’re not waving goodbye to the homeland, you want to come back eventually?

Mpaki: Never, I definitely want to come back. We need to develop our own country, developing South Africa and developing Africa as a whole.

V/O: But not everyone has the same vision.

Derek: Would you consider at some stage returning to South Africa, and under what conditions?

Promise: No never. Never. I'm never coming back home. Because I feel like no one is saving us. No one is doing anything to save us. So many things are happening and we see them happening but no one is accountable for anything. I was born in 93 – post-apartheid. But I still feel like whatever that was oppressing people then is oppressing us just on a different racial level. No I know I'm never. I’m dying here. Save plane ticket money – you’re going to bury me here.
